# Connect to a database (MCP) {#sec-mcp}

Ask an agent for "recent papers on TCF-1 and chromatin in T cells" and it will answer
from memory. That memory is large, and it is often right, but it is frozen at the date
the model was trained, and it has no way to tell a paper it read from a paper that merely
sounds plausible. Language models are known to invent references: in one study, 18% of
the citations GPT-4 produced for short literature reviews did not exist, and a quarter
of the real ones had substantive errors [@doi:10.1038/s41598-023-41032-5]. Newer models
are better at saying "I don't know", but "better" is not a standard you can cite.

The fix is not a cleverer prompt. It is to let the agent **ask the system of record**:
search PubMed itself, get back real PMIDs, and show you where each fact came from. The
**Model Context Protocol (MCP)** is how that connection is made
[@url:https://modelcontextprotocol.io/]. An MCP server sits in front of a database or
service and offers the agent a handful of tools, such as "search articles" or "get
article metadata". The agent decides when to call them and what to ask. You add the
server once, and from then on it is part of what the agent can do.

In @sec-skills you gave the agent *instructions*: how your lab triages a results table.
A skill tells the agent **how**. An MCP server tells it **what is there now**. This
chapter connects one server, PubMed, which needs no account, and then does the thing
that matters most: checks what came back.

## What you'll learn

- What an MCP server is, and how it differs from a skill.
- How to connect the PubMed server, three ways: by asking the agent, from the command
  line, or as a plugin from Anthropic's life-sciences marketplace.
- How to compare an answer from memory with an answer from a live database.
- How to check retrieved results by hand, and why retrieval is not the same as truth.
- What an MCP server can see, and which servers to trust.

## How an MCP connection works

An MCP server is a small program, usually run by whoever owns the data, that speaks one
agreed protocol. When your agent starts, it asks each configured server "what tools do
you have?" and gets back a list with names, descriptions and inputs. From then on,
whenever a question needs one of those tools, the agent calls it, reads the result and
carries on (@fig-mcp-flow).

```{mermaid}
%%| label: fig-mcp-flow
%%| fig-cap: "One question, answered through the PubMed MCP server. The agent chooses
%%|   the tools and the search terms; the server turns each call into a query against
%%|   PubMed and returns the records."
sequenceDiagram
    participant You
    participant Agent
    participant Server as PubMed MCP server
    participant PubMed
    You->>Agent: Find papers on TCF-1 and 3D genome
    Agent->>Server: search_articles("TCF-1 AND chromatin …")
    Server->>PubMed: search
    PubMed-->>Server: matching PMIDs
    Server-->>Agent: PMIDs
    Agent->>Server: get_article_metadata([PMIDs])
    Server-->>Agent: titles, authors, journals
    Agent-->>You: three papers, with PMIDs and sources
```

::: {.column-margin}
**Protocol**: an agreed way for two programs to talk. Because MCP is shared, the same
PubMed server works with Claude Code, Claude's desktop app, Gemini CLI, Codex and
Copilot. Only the place you configure it differs.
:::

Two things follow from this picture. First, **the agent writes the query**. You asked
in plain English; the agent turned that into search terms, and a search can match the
wrong organism, the wrong assay or the wrong TCF (there are several). Second, **the
server sees your question**, or at least the parts of it the agent sends. Both come
back later in this chapter.

@tbl-mcp-vs-skill sets MCP beside the skill you wrote in @sec-skills.

| | Skill (@sec-skills) | MCP server (this chapter) |
|---|---|---|
| What it is | A folder of instructions, perhaps with scripts | A live connection to another system |
| What it adds | *How* to do a task your way | *What is there*, now: records, data |
| Where it runs | On your machine, inside the agent's session | On someone's server, usually |
| What leaves your machine | Nothing beyond the usual | Whatever the agent sends in its tool calls |
| Example | `deseq2-triage` | PubMed, Open Targets |

: A skill and an MCP server do different jobs, and they combine: a skill can tell the
agent which server to use and how to check its results. {#tbl-mcp-vs-skill}

### Anthropic's life-sciences servers

Anthropic keeps a list of MCP servers and skills for life sciences in a public GitHub
repository, packaged as Claude Code **plugins** in a **marketplace**
[@url:https://github.com/anthropics/life-sciences]. A plugin is a bundle; a marketplace
is a list of plugins you can install by name. The servers themselves are run by the
data providers, not by Anthropic. @tbl-mcp-servers lists the ones most useful to this
room, and only claims what we checked on 23 September 2026.

| Plugin | Reaches | Account | What we checked |
|---|---|---|---|
| `pubmed` | PubMed and PubMed Central (NLM) | None | Connected, listed 7 tools, answered real queries |
| `open-targets` | Open Targets Platform: target–disease evidence | None found | Connected, answered a real query that matched the website's API |
| `biorxiv` | bioRxiv and medRxiv preprints | Not stated | Not checked: refused our test request (403), which may be bot-blocking |
| `chembl` | ChEMBL bioactive compounds | Not stated | Not checked, as above |
| `clinical-trials` | ClinicalTrials.gov | Not stated | Not checked, as above |
| `biorender`, `synapse`, `wiley-scholar-gateway`, `consensus` | Figures; Sage data; Wiley papers; paper search | Free account | Not checked; account needs from the repository's README |
| `10x-genomics`, `cortellis`, `adisinsight` | 10x Cloud; drug regulation; drug pipelines | Paid or institutional | Not checked; from the README |

: Some of the MCP servers in `anthropics/life-sciences`. The repository also carries
skills (single-cell QC, nf-core pipelines, scvi-tools), which are the kind of thing you
met in @sec-skills. {#tbl-mcp-servers}

**PubMed is not in the official Anthropic marketplace** that Claude Code sets up for
you. To install it as a plugin you add the life-sciences marketplace first. The simpler
route, which works in every tool, is to give the agent the server's address directly.

## Worked example

We asked the same question twice, in two empty folders, with web search and the shell
turned off so the only route to PubMed was MCP. First, with no server connected:

```default
Find three papers on how TCF-1 (Tcf7) shapes 3D genome organisation or chromatin in
T cells. For each give the first author, year, journal, title and PMID. Say where each
fact came from.
```

The bare agent was careful. It said it had no way to look anything up, gave three
papers from memory, and **left the PMIDs blank**, "because I don't remember them
reliably, and a made-up PMID is worse than a blank". All three papers turned out to be
real. But you could not have known that from the answer, and without PMIDs you had to do
the searching yourself.

Then we connected PubMed in the second folder, using the `.mcp.json` file you'll write
in a moment, and asked again. This time the agent searched PubMed twice
(`search_articles`) and fetched the records it found (`get_article_metadata`), and came
back in about 30 seconds with @tbl-mcp-worked.

| First author, year | Journal | Title (shortened) | PMID |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wang, 2022 | *Nat Immunol* | TCF-1 promotes chromatin interactions across TADs in T cell progenitors | 35726060 |
| Shan, 2022 | *Nat Immunol* | Tcf1–CTCF cooperativity shapes genomic architecture … | 35882936 |
| Johnson, 2018 | *Immunity* | Lineage-determining TF TCF-1 initiates the epigenetic identity of T cells | 29466756 |

: What the agent returned with PubMed connected [@pmid:35726060; @pmid:35882936;
@pmid:29466756]. {#tbl-mcp-worked}

Just as useful was what it said about its own work:

- It picked papers 1 and 3 **from their titles alone**, and said so: "I didn't read its
  abstract."
- Paper 2 did not come up in its broad search. It **remembered** the paper, searched
  for it by name, and took every detail from the PubMed record. It said that too.
- Paper 3 is about chromatin accessibility, not 3D structure, which it flagged as a
  partial fit.

Then we checked. We looked up all three PMIDs directly in PubMed, independently of the
agent: every title, first author, journal and year matched. We also checked the paper
the bare agent had remembered but the connected one did not use (Shan 2021, *Nat
Commun*); it is real too [@pmid:34615872].

So memory did not fail here, and that is the honest result. **What changed is that the
answer became checkable**: every claim came with an identifier and a stated source, and
the agent separated what it had read from what it had inferred from a title.

::: {.callout-note}
## Is the second paper really about 3D genome structure?

The agent read that abstract and quoted it: Tcf1 and CTCF together "promote chromatin
interactions and form highly connected, dynamic interaction hubs". That is a claim about
the paper, not a PMID, and checking it means reading the abstract yourself. That is the
part of the check that no tool does for you.
:::

## Your turn

You'll need about 20 minutes. Use your workshop folder from [Setup](00-setup.qmd), or make a new
folder for this chapter.

::: {.callout-warning}
## What leaves your machine

Every tool call sends the agent's query to the server's operator. For PubMed that means
your search terms: a topic, gene names, a disease. That is usually fine. Don't put
anything in a query you wouldn't type into the PubMed website: no patient details, and
nothing about unpublished work you've been asked to keep quiet.
:::

### 1. Ask first, without a connection

Pick a topic you know well enough to judge an answer: your own field, a method you use,
a gene you study. Start a new session and ask:

```default
Find three recent papers on <your topic>. For each give the first author, year,
journal, title and PMID. Say where each fact came from. Don't search the web.
```

"Don't search the web" matters: Claude Code can search the web, and today you want
to see what it knows **without** a database. Copy the answer into your ledger
(@sec-ledger) under *Asked*.

No topic in mind? Use ours: the question in the worked example. Or use genes from the
Vahedi lab's RNA-seq data: the top hits in `differential_genes.tsv`, from their
repository's `track-a/data/README.md`, are Jun, Myc, Irf4 and Ccr7, in B cells lacking a
CTCF binding site ([Vahedi lab repository](https://github.com/golnazvahedi/epigenetics-agentic-workshop)).

### 2. Connect PubMed

Choose **one** route (@tbl-mcp-routes). If you're not sure, use route A: the agent does
the work, and it works in the desktop app and the command line alike.

| Route | Best if you use | You type | Where it's saved |
|---|---|---|---|
| A. Ask the agent | Anything | A prompt | `.mcp.json` in this folder |
| B. Command line | `claude` in a terminal | One command | `.mcp.json` in this folder |
| C. Plugin | Claude Code | Two commands, or the plugin browser | Your user settings: every folder |

: Three ways to connect the same server. A and B only affect this folder, which is
what you want for a first try. {#tbl-mcp-routes}

**Route A: ask the agent.** In a session in your workshop folder, paste:

```default
Create a file called .mcp.json in this folder, containing exactly:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "pubmed": {
      "type": "http",
      "url": "https://pubmed.mcp.claude.com/mcp"
    }
  }
}

Then tell me the full path of the file.
```

This is the project-level MCP file Claude Code reads, in the documented format
[@url:https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp]. The desktop app's Code tab reads the same
file. Then **start a new session in the same folder**: servers are loaded when a session
starts. Claude Code asks you to approve a server from `.mcp.json` the first time it
sees it. Approve it; you've read what's in it. (In the desktop app, check on the day
exactly how that approval appears.)

**Route B: the command line.** In a terminal, in your workshop folder:

```bash
claude mcp add --transport http pubmed --scope project https://pubmed.mcp.claude.com/mcp
```

It writes the same `.mcp.json` as route A. Leave out `--scope project` and it's saved in
your personal settings instead, for this folder only. Then run `claude` and approve the
server when asked.

**Route C: a plugin from the life-sciences marketplace.** In Claude Code, type:

```default
/plugin marketplace add anthropics/life-sciences
/plugin install pubmed@life-sciences
```

The first command adds the marketplace, the second installs PubMed from it. By default
this installs it for **you**, in every folder, not just this one. We tested the same two
steps from the shell (`claude plugin marketplace add …`, then `claude plugin install …`)
and the server connected. In the desktop app, plugins live under the **+** button, then
**Plugins**, then **Add plugin**, which browses the marketplaces you've already added.
Whether you can add a *new* marketplace from there, check on the day. If not, use
route A.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Using Gemini CLI, Codex or Copilot?

The server is the same; only the configuration file differs. Ask your agent: "Add a
remote HTTP MCP server called pubmed, at https://pubmed.mcp.claude.com/mcp, to your own
MCP configuration for this folder, and tell me which file you changed." Then check the
file it names.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## On Windows

- **Let the agent create `.mcp.json` (route A).** The name starts with a dot and File
  Explorer hides extensions by default, so a file made in Notepad can end up called
  `.mcp.json.txt` and be silently ignored.
- Route B works in PowerShell or CMD once `claude` is installed.
- Plugins aren't available in WSL sessions. See @sec-windows.
:::

::: {.callout-important}
## If the connection is blocked

Organisations can restrict which marketplaces and servers their members may add. If a
route fails with a message about policy or permissions, that isn't you doing something
wrong. Try route A, and if that's blocked too, ask whoever runs your Claude account.
:::

### 3. Check what the agent can now do

In the new session, ask:

```default
Which MCP servers are connected, and what tools does each one give you?
```

You should see a PubMed server with seven tools: `search_articles`,
`get_article_metadata`, `find_related_articles`, `lookup_article_by_citation`,
`convert_article_ids`, `get_full_text_article` and `get_copyright_status`. In the
command line, `/mcp` lists each server with its status and number of tools. If PubMed isn't
listed, see "If it goes wrong" below.

::: {.callout-note}
## Two PubMed servers?

Servers added to your claude.ai account as **connectors** also appear in Claude Code
when you're signed in with that account. On Team and Enterprise plans only admins can
add them. So you may see a "claude.ai PubMed" as well as the one you just added. They
reach the same database; either will do.
:::

### 4. Ask again, with the database

Ask exactly the question from step 1, but take out "Don't search the web" and add:

```default
Use PubMed. For each paper, say whether you read the abstract or chose it from the
title alone.
```

Put the two answers side by side. What's different: the papers, the PMIDs, how sure
the agent sounds, what it says about where each fact came from?

### 5. Check three PMIDs by hand

This is the step that counts. For three of the papers, open
`https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/<PMID>/` in your browser, putting the PMID in place of
`<PMID>`, and check:

1. **Does the PMID exist**, and is it the paper the agent named: title, first author,
   year?
2. **Is it about what you asked?** Right organism, right assay, right gene? A search for
   "TCF" can find the wrong TCF.
3. **Does the abstract support what the agent said about it?** Read it. This is the
   check no tool can do for you.

Then write a ledger entry. *Checked how* is the three PMIDs and what you found, and
*Confidently wrong* is anything that didn't hold up.

### If it goes wrong

| What you see | What to try |
|---|---|
| PubMed isn't in the tool list | Start a **new** session in the same folder; servers load at start. |
| "Pending approval" | Run `claude` in the folder and approve the server, or start a new desktop session there. |
| The agent searches the web instead | Say "Use the PubMed tools, not web search." |
| `.mcp.json` is somewhere else | Ask "What folder are you in?" The file must sit in the folder the session was started in. |
| A plugin command is "unknown" | Update Claude Code, or use route A. |

: Common problems when connecting a server. {#tbl-mcp-troubleshoot}

## What to notice

- **The agent chose the tools and wrote the queries.** You never saw PubMed's search
  syntax. That's convenient, and it's also where silent errors come from: look at the
  search terms it used (ask it) before trusting that "no papers found" means none
  exist.
- **Retrieval is not truth.** A real PMID proves the paper exists. It doesn't prove the
  paper says what the agent claims, or that it's the best paper on the topic. The agent
  in our worked example chose two papers from their titles and said so. Ask yours to do
  the same.
- **The good answer showed its sources.** Compare how each answer said where its facts
  came from. That, more than the facts, is what the connection bought.
- **You added a capability without writing code.** Four lines of JSON, and the agent
  can now search a database it couldn't reach before.

## Check yourself

You're done when:

- [ ] the agent lists the PubMed server and its tools;
- [ ] you have two answers to the same question, one from memory and one from PubMed;
- [ ] you have opened three PMIDs on the PubMed website and checked them against what
  the agent said;
- [ ] your ledger has an entry saying what you checked and what you found.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Which servers to trust

A server you connect can see every query the agent sends it, and its answers go straight
into the agent's work. Content a server returns can even contain instructions aimed at
the agent (a *prompt injection*), which is why Claude Code's documentation says to
verify you trust each server before connecting it
[@url:https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp]. Plugins are trusted more still: they can run
code on your machine.

- Install servers from the data's owner or from a source you trust, such as the NLM, the
  Open Targets consortium or Anthropic's own list, not from a random repository.
- For servers that need an account, **treat the token like a password**. Don't paste it
  into the chat, and don't put it in a `.mcp.json` you'll share or commit.
- Your institution's rules on data still apply. A connection doesn't change what you're
  allowed to send.
:::

## Going further

- **A second database.** Add Open Targets to the same `.mcp.json`, as a second entry
  under `"mcpServers"` with `"url": "https://mcp.platform.opentargets.org/mcp"`, and ask:
  "Using Open Targets, what are the top five diseases associated with the human gene
  IRF4, with their overall association scores?" When we tried it, the answer matched
  Open Targets' own API exactly. Then check one of the diseases on
  [platform.opentargets.org](https://platform.opentargets.org): which kinds of evidence
  hold its score up?
- **Two databases, one question.** With both connected, ask a question that needs both:
  "For the top five IRF4-associated diseases in Open Targets, find one recent review
  for each in PubMed."
- **A skill that uses a server.** Combine this chapter with @sec-skills: a skill that
  says "when asked for literature, use PubMed, give PMIDs, and say which abstracts you
  read".
- **Build your own server.** The Vahedi lab's afternoon has a pod on exactly this:
  wiring up a server, or having the agent write a small one around a public API such as
  Ensembl or GEO:
  [Pod 2, Connect to the outside world](https://github.com/golnazvahedi/epigenetics-agentic-workshop/blob/main/track-b/pod-2-mcp-connections.md).
- **Undo it.** Delete `.mcp.json`, or run `claude mcp remove pubmed -s project`. A plugin
  can be uninstalled from `/plugin`, or from **Manage plugins** in the desktop app.
